Itinérance dans l’est de Montréal : une: Homelessness in Montréal’s East End: A Silent Crisis
Dans l’est de Montréal, l’itinérance pre: In Montréal’s east end, homelessness is growing, now reaching neighbourhoods that until recently were relatively spared.
Entrée des résidents au refuge du CAP Sa: Entrance for residents at the CAP Saint-Barnabé shelter. Photo: Jennifer Da Veiga Rocha
Lorsqu’on traite d’itinérance, le Centre: When we talk about homelessness, Montréal’s Centre-Sud often gets all the attention. Yet other neighbourhoods deserve a closer look. Since the pandemic, precarity has spread across the island, including the east end.
Avant 2020, il n’existait aucun refuge d: Before 2020, there was no shelter in this part of the city. CAP Saint-Barnabé initially offered 15 spots when it opened, and today takes in up to 350 people. Even so, about fifty requests are turned away every day for lack of space.
Plus loin dans l’est, la situation est e: Farther east, the situation is even more critical. In Mercier-Est, there is only one day centre, and in Pointe-aux-Trembles, a warming centre opened late, on January 20, when winter was already well underway. This resource is open only once or twice a week, and only for a few hours. Outside of the warming centre, there is nowhere to sleep or eat. A housing project is planned, but it won’t see the light of day for another two years.
Au départ, je voulais aussi couvrir la s: At first, I also wanted to cover the situation in Montréal-Nord, but the borough’s only shelter isn’t willing to speak to the media at this time.
Pour réaliser ce reportage, j’ai été acc: To produce this report, I was accompanied by Yseult Picard, a former journalist at L’Itinéraire. I want to thank her for her time and research. Finding information is not easy; resources are lacking.
Yseult a pris le temps de faire des appe: Yseult took the time to make calls, sometimes even to related organizations, so that we could be pointed toward centres involved in the fight against homelessness. That is how we found out that in Pointe-aux-Trembles, an organization originally dedicated to crime prevention also employs a homelessness outreach worker, the only one in the area.
Ce reportage ne porte donc que sur une p: This report therefore covers only part of the Montréal territory, but I hope it will help people better understand the precarity taking hold in the east end and the urgency of finding solutions.
<strong><em>Dans l’est de Montréal, l’it: In Montréal’s east end, homelessness is growing, now reaching neighbourhoods that until recently were relatively spared. While needs are rising at an alarming rate, emergency resources remain largely inadequate. The few shelters and community organizations in the area are under growing pressure. How can they respond to a crisis that exceeds their capacity? La Converse went to meet the people working on the ground, visiting the only shelter in Montréal’s east end and speaking with outreach workers who operate between Hochelaga and Pointe-aux-Trembles. Report.
<strong>Mercredi 29 janvier.</strong> Il: Wednesday, January 29. It is 9 a.m., and we are not far from Viau station. In front of the doors of the CAP Saint-Barnabé shelter, the sun shines high in the sky, but its deceptive light warms nothing.
Une dizaine de silhouettes sont dehors,: About ten silhouettes stand outside near the entrance, each with a cigarette in hand. Their movements are quick, almost frantic, as if smoking had become a race against the frost. Among them is Jeff, a Haitian man who grew up in the United States and arrived in Quebec on his own about ten years ago. Bundled up in a thick coat and winter boots, he is smiling. “I only got here in September,” he begins. Incarcerated after an altercation with his former roommates, he lost his housing as well as his job. “I lived really close by,” he continues. “But now, I hope to find a job quickly, then a place to live. I don’t plan on staying here long,” he says.
Autour de lui, certains ne sont pas auss: Around him, some are not as well protected against the winter. Running shoes with holes, sandals without socks, jackets that are too thin. The cold spares no one; it seeps through worn clothing. A few more minutes, and they will be back in the shelter’s warmth.
<strong>Hochelaga : le seul refuge de l’: Hochelaga: the only shelter in the east end
Michelle Patenaude, directrice générale: Michelle Patenaude, the shelter’s executive director, welcomes us inside. Here, everyone seems to like her. The centre, located in a former arena, offers an impressive space: more than 192 numbered cubicles are lined up, each equipped with a bed and a table. “These are army cots,” she explains with a laugh, as if to lighten the situation.
Avant de se retrouver à la tête de l’org: Before taking the helm of the organization, Michelle was its clinical coordinator. She witnessed the place grow, especially during the pandemic. “We’re the only shelter in the east end, and we grew fast. Back then, CAP Saint-Barnabé was just a food security organization. We did emergency assistance, we had a small community grocery store. People came to eat, and a lot of them were from the neighbourhood, not necessarily people experiencing homelessness, but also people who were at risk of becoming homeless,” she says.
Puis la pandémie a tout bouleversé. « Ç’: Then the pandemic upended everything. “It exploded. Before, there was a lot of couchsurfing, meaning hidden homelessness. People slept temporarily at friends’ places, or in the rooming houses on Maisonneuve. But when the apartments where they hung out were closed, boarded up, they were left with no solution.”
À cela s’est ajoutée la crise des opioïd: On top of that came the opioid crisis, renovictions, the closure of seniors’ residences and the conversion of CHSLDs into maisons des aînés, the shelter’s director explains. “All of that made homelessness far more visible.”
Au départ, le refuge ne comptait que 15: At the start, the shelter had only 15 spots – 7 for women and 8 for men – and was open Monday to Friday. The director still remembers how nonsensical that was, “as if homelessness went away on weekends,” she says sarcastically.
Cubicule numéroté du refuge CAP Saint-Ba: A numbered cubicle at the CAP Saint-Barnabé shelter. Photo: Jennifer Da Veiga Rocha
Aujourd’hui, la capacité d’accueil a exp: Today, capacity has exploded: 350 spots are offered in total, spread across the shelter’s three sites. In addition to the 192 spots at this first site, 50 spots are available at the second site, on rue Benette, with a night drop-in in winter, and 90 spots on rue De Chambly. “We’ve just added spots for 30 more people, which brings us to 380 spots right now,” she continues. At the back of the arena, several red garden chairs have been added for those who don’t have a bed.
Mais malgré cette croissance, le manque: But despite this growth, the lack of space remains a daily emergency. “Yesterday, we had to turn away 52 people. We were full. These people didn’t get a bed, or even a spot at a drop-in,” Michelle Patenaude says with regret.
M. Eduard* passe devant nous en poussant: Mr. Eduard* walks past us pushing a stroller in which his “baby” sleeps, Princesse the dog, his faithful companion for 14 years. With his Trilby hat, warm coat, fleece jacket zipped up to his chin and enormous ring on his ring finger, the man, who is in his sixties, appears to be doing well. Yet we quickly understand that his life is anything but easy.
Arrivé au Canada en 1996, ce Roumain qui: Arriving in Canada in 1996, this Romanian man, who says he is stateless, filed a claim for political asylum that was reportedly rejected in 1998. Since then, he has lived without status, which leaves him in a very precarious economic situation. “I’ve been here 30 years without working legally,” he sighs. For 17 years, he lived with two of his now-adult children in a 4½ in Villeray. Then, within a few months, everything collapsed: health problems, several heart attacks, a long hospital stay and a family breakup... The result? He lost his home and has lived at the shelter since 2020.
Comment survit-il ? « Grâce à Dieu », ré: How does he survive? “Thanks to God,” replies the man who lost everything except his faith. He gets by and considers the shelter his home.
Pour se rendre au bureau de Michelle, il: To get to Michelle’s office, you have to leave the shelter and go to the front of the building. The office is bright and quiet, and two parrots perched at the entrance punctuate our conversation. For a few years now, Eduard hasn’t been the only one staying at the shelter. “There are people who have been here since the Notre-Dame Street encampment was dismantled in 2020. This is their home. It’s where they live.” She stresses those last words.
La multiplication des hébergements d’urg: The multiplication of emergency shelters during the pandemic led to an increase in chronic homelessness, Michelle explains. “We opened a lot of shelters without asking how to help people regain long-term stability. As a result, many got stuck in these services with no real way out.”
Certaines organisations ont alors essayé: Some organizations then tried to turn these places into transitional housing by adding programs to help people regain some stability more quickly. Michelle explains, however, that CAP Saint-Barnabé’s primary mission is to respond to emergencies, which makes it hard to put such programs in place. “I’m really managing the emergency of the emergency. It becomes hard to go further in the services we offer at that point. And people end up falling into chronic homelessness.”
She adds: “And it’s understandable. Imagine: you have no family, no friends, no children; you find yourself in a shelter where, even if you don’t talk to anyone, there are people around you. It’s reassuring.”
Rassurant au point que certains, une foi: So reassuring that some, once in housing, are ready to give up their comfort to find a bit of human warmth, she explains. “Some time ago, we placed someone in an apartment. Unfortunately, the apartment was near Papineau metro. The man kept coming to ask us if we had housing in Hochelaga, he insisted and was ready to give up his apartment, even if it meant coming back to the shelter. Simply because his friends, his network, everything was here.”
Pour répondre à ce besoin, le refuge che: To meet this need, the shelter is looking to acquire two buildings in the neighbourhood. “One of them has 20 units. We’re going to take it, we’re going to take care of it. It’s essential to stay here, where people want to be.”
Mais la crise du logement complique les: But the housing crisis complicates things. “With the projected 5.9% rent increase, people who are already vulnerable are in even more danger. I have couples who can’t find housing because, as soon as they find an apartment, their social assistance is reduced and they can no longer survive financially,” she says.
Et la situation ne s’améliore pas. Cet é: And the situation isn’t improving. This summer, the Chambly site, which houses 90 people, will have to close. The building has been sold, forcing the shelter to leave the premises.
« Le financement, c’est toujours une inq: “Funding is always a worry. And in 2026, what’s going to happen? The crisis isn’t going to resolve itself by miracle,” Michelle says bitterly.
« On parle de diriger les personnes itin: “There’s talk of directing people experiencing homelessness to the various Montréal resources. But those aren’t up to speed and, above all, people don’t want to be uprooted. You can’t impose a place to live on them. Like everyone, they want to choose where they live. They already have so few choices…” she says.
À 14 km du refuge du CAP Saint-Barnabé,: Fourteen kilometres from the CAP Saint-Barnabé shelter, we meet Michel Dorais in his office. He is a homelessness outreach worker with the organization Prévention Pointe-de-l’Île (PPDI). Dressed in an electric blue shirt, this tall man with a kind gaze is the only person dealing with homelessness in this area.
Depuis le 20 janvier 2025, il gère une p: Since January 20, 2025, he has run a small warming centre, an unmarked space meant for the few people experiencing homelessness whom he knows. Inside, five people find a bit of respite once or twice a week, but only for a few hours. These people have nowhere else to go. The nearest shelter, CAP Saint-Barnabé, is several hours away on foot.
Avant la pandémie, l’itinérance était un: Before the pandemic, homelessness was an invisible reality in the neighbourhood, he says. “People often gathered, several at a time, in the same apartment.” But like the rest of Montréal, the Pointe-aux-Trembles neighbourhood has not been spared by the crisis.
Pourtant, ce n’est qu’en 2023 qu’un fina: Yet it was only in 2023 that funding was freed up for a homelessness outreach position in Pointe-aux-Trembles.
Le téléphone de Michel sonne. Un homme l: Michel’s phone rings. A man is calling him. After a short conversation, he comes back to us. “That’s David*, a person experiencing homelessness. He’s in the parking lot of the Galeries Tricentenaire. He called to tell me he’s hungry, that he hasn’t eaten since yesterday. I’m going to get him a McDo.” Michel then puts on yet another of his many hats.
« Comme je suis le seul intervenant en i: “Since I’m the only homelessness outreach worker, I can’t just direct them to other services. And there’s nothing here: no food, no place to sleep or warm up. If I refer them elsewhere, the organizations tell them to come to them. But they won’t go, they won’t take several buses and a metro to get there.”
Michel pallie alors lui-même ces failles: Michel therefore fills these gaps himself, bringing resources directly to those who reach out to him. Or sometimes he drives them all the way downtown so they can finally get help. “Without support, they can’t make it,” he sighs.
<strong>Rester ou partir : quand les res: Stay or leave: when resources fall short
À ce jour, Pointe-aux-Trembles compte un: To date, Pointe-aux-Trembles has about ten visibly homeless people, the outreach worker reports. And as many people in precarious situations, close to the breaking point. But unlike downtown, no services are dedicated to them here. “So they leave, come back, then often end up abandoning the area,” Michel continues. “If we see only about ten people experiencing homelessness here, it’s not because there are ‘only 10’; some prefer to go downtown because they want a certain dignity. Others, on the other hand, categorically refuse to leave the neighbourhood.”
« Ces personnes, poursuit-il, passent la: “These people,” he continues, “spend the night in bank ATM vestibules, for lack of anything better.” Support services are too far away.
Sur ces mots, nous quittons son bureau p: With that, we leave his office to go meet David*, who is waiting for Michel in the shopping centre parking lot.
Sur place, on aperçoit une chaise de cam: On site, we spot an empty camping chair. Michel knows where to look. He heads without hesitation to a nearby convenience store. A few minutes later, he comes out with a man bundled up in a ski suit. A toque and hood pulled down over his head, he has long blond hair, a full beard and piercing blue eyes. The man, in his fifties, is a former construction worker.
Pour survivre, il a adopté une approche: To survive, he has adopted a two-part approach. “At night, I sleep at the foot of a heated building; and during the day, I come here. I don’t panhandle, but people sometimes give me a few coins to eat,” he sums up.
Très brièvement, il évoque ce qui l’a am: Very briefly, he talks about what led him to homelessness: a family conflict, but mostly, in his view, the government. “I hate the government,” he says. “I’ve always worked. Now they give me a miserable welfare cheque. If I want to retire, I have to wait another 11 years. And since I’m in this situation, my pension will shrink too,” he says bitterly.
Malgré la dureté de sa condition et l’ab: Despite the harshness of his condition and the lack of help in the neighbourhood, his answer is unequivocal when asked if he wouldn’t prefer to go downtown: “No, I’m not leaving Pointe-aux-Trembles. I’m from here, I grew up here.”
C’est pour des personnes comme David que: It is for people like David that Michel would like to see more services in the neighbourhood. A project is underway, he says. “It should take about two years,” he continues, before people experiencing homelessness in Pointe-aux-Trembles finally have a place to sleep, eat and wash.
Dans le quartier de Mercier-Est, dans l’: In the Mercier-Est neighbourhood, in Montréal’s east end, is the day centre Le PAS de la rue. For more than 20 years, this organization has welcomed, supported and accompanied people aged 55 and over who are experiencing homelessness.
Chaque jour, plus de 200 repas chauds so: Every day, Le PAS de la rue serves more than 200 hot meals, split between its two day centres, one in Mercier and the other in the Centre-Sud neighbourhood. But beyond the food, what is offered to these seniors, who are often left behind, is a presence, a listening ear and support.
Parmi les figures familières de l’organi: Among the organization’s familiar faces is Dany Ayotte Kelly, a community outreach worker. “Homelessness in Montréal’s east end is less visible than elsewhere, but it’s very real. There’s a lot of hidden homelessness: people who sleep in their cars or go from couch to couch at acquaintances’ places. They’re invisible, but they exist and they need help,” he insists.
Dans des quartiers comme Tétreaultville: In neighbourhoods like Tétreaultville and Mercier-Est, couchsurfing at 55 or 60 is commonplace, he says. These people, who no longer have a fixed address, go from one place to another until the street becomes their only option. And once they’re outside, going back is hard.
Chaque matin, Dany enfile ses bottes et: Every morning, Dany pulls on his boots and walks the streets of Mercier. He goes by Joliette metro, as far as Honoré-Beaugrand station, and sometimes pushes on to Anjou, to meet those who have nothing left. “I go to them, where they are: in metro stations, in front of stores, in makeshift encampments. The idea is to build a bond of trust and direct them to the appropriate resources,” he explains.
Mais le plus grand défi n’est pas de tro: But the biggest challenge is not finding a shelter or a hot meal. “Many of these seniors have lost faith in society. They’ve been through many breakdowns, abandonments, humiliations. Our work is also about repairing those broken bonds, giving them back some trust. One step at a time, one person at a time.”
« Ils font face à beaucoup de solitude f: “They face a lot of loneliness when it comes to family. Sometimes, we’re their only network. Right now, we’re supporting a senior at the end of life, with no family, whose only support is the outreach workers he has met over the years. Watching him go alone is heartbreaking. But we’re here, until the end,” says Dany, visibly very moved.
Au cours de l’été 2024, une nouvelle vag: In the summer of 2024, a new wave of homelessness swept through seniors. The housing crisis was a real catalyst: people who were already in precarious situations saw their last line of defence fall. “Living in a rooming house often means living in permanent instability. Conditions are hard, and basic needs aren’t met. Every day we receive more and more requests for help,” Dany points out.
Pour Dany, c’est le même constat : l’est: For Dany, it’s the same observation: Montréal’s east end is particularly underserved. Few shelters, too few day centres, a shortage of food banks. Refusals at CAP Saint-Barnabé are commonplace because of the lack of space. “We can multiply warming centres all we want, everything is always full. When I have to tell someone, ‘I have nowhere to take you,’ I know I’m reinforcing their belief that no one will come to help them. It’s terrible.”
En 2021, Le PAS de la rue aidait une vin: In 2021, Le PAS de la rue helped about twenty people a day. In 2024, that number climbed to 50, sometimes 65. The deterioration in living conditions for vulnerable seniors is dramatic. “We see people who had never experienced homelessness before. People who had housing, a stable life, and who, because of rent increases and a string of bad luck, end up on the street. When everything collapses – job, housing, health – there’s not much left,” Dany laments.
Malgré tout, l’intervenant reste motivé: Despite everything, the outreach worker stays motivated by the human connection. “The beauty of this work is being there for them. These are people who no longer believe in human contact, in the hope of an outstretched hand. But by showing them that we don’t judge them, that we won’t betray them, we sometimes manage to break through that shell.”
Alors que les acteurs sur le terrain red: As those working on the ground redouble their efforts to support the most vulnerable, one question remains: how long can they hold on without a stronger commitment from the authorities, while homelessness in Montréal’s east end continues to grow?
